overview.title: 📖 Overview: Exclusions, Exaggerations, and Deadlines
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 57a–57b
overview.hebrewSource: הַכֹּל נִכְנָסִין לַדִּיר לְהִתְעַשֵּׂר, חוּץ מִן כִּלְאַיִם, וּטְרֵפָה, וְיוֹצֵא דּוֹפֶן, וּמְחוּסַּר זְמַן, וְהַיָּתוֹם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by confirming why Rabbi Yoḥanan's rulings — that divided brothers are like purchasers of land, and that purchased fetuses still enter the pen — both needed to be stated independently. A new mishna then lists which animals are excluded from animal tithe altogether: a crossbred (kilayim), a tereifa, one born by caesarean section, one too young, and an 'orphan' whose mother died in childbirth — defining that last category precisely via Rabbi Yehoshua's view about the mother's hide. The Gemara derives these exclusions from the same 'under' verbal analogy used for sacrificial animals, then notes that certain disqualified-for-the-altar animals (from illicit unions or idol worship) are nonetheless included in tithe, since a blemish alone doesn't disqualify tithe. A colorful digression records outsized testimonies about the natural world before the daf turns to a new mishna: Rabbi Akiva's three yearly gathering times for animal tithe.

slides.title: 🐕 Why Two Separate Teachings Were Needed
slides.label: Rabbi Yoḥanan's rulings, and why neither alone would suffice:
slides.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan taught both that brothers who divide an inheritance are considered purchasers from each other (obligating them to return shares in the Jubilee), and separately that purchased fetuses still enter the pen for animal tithe. Had only the Jubilee ruling been stated, one might think it applies uniquely because land must physically 'return' to its original state. Had only the animal-tithe ruling been stated, one might think brothers are treated as receiving their own designated share retroactively. Both statements together close off each possible limitation.

slides.title: 🚫 Five Categories Excluded from Animal Tithe
slides.subtitle: The mishna's list and its scriptural source
rows: 'A bull OR a sheep' — excludes a mixed-species offspring
'OR a goat' — excludes a lamb that looks like a goat, or vice versa
'Then it shall be SEVEN DAYS' — excludes one whose time hasn't arrived
'UNDER its mother' — excludes an animal with no mother present

callout.label: Verbal analogy:
callout.text: Rabbi Yishmael, son of R' Yoḥanan ben Beroka, links 'under the rod' (tithe) to 'under its mother' (offerings) — each category excludes the other's cases too, including a tereifa on both sides.

slides.title: 🐄 Disqualified for the Altar, Yet Still Tithed
slides.subtitle: The mishna's expansive 'all' includes surprising cases

boxes.title: Why the Difference?
items: Animal tithe is never disqualified by a mere blemish ('he shall not inspect between good and bad')
So corruption-based disqualifications don't apply to tithe either

boxes.title: The Exception
items: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda: tumtum and androginus ARE excluded
Reason: their SEX is uncertain, and sacrificial animals require a definite male or female — like a tereifa, excluded by 'under the rod' itself

slides.title: 🗣️ Testimonies from the Edge of the Empire
slides.label: Rabbi Yishmael ben Satriel's reports to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi:
slides.text: In our locale, they flay a dead mother's hide to clothe her newborn — explaining why the mishna's 'orphan' exemption depends on whether the hide survives. Our lettuce has 600,000 leaves in its stalk. Once a cedar fell so wide that sixteen wagons passed over its trunk side by side. Once an unfertilized egg of the bar yokhani bird fell, drowning sixty cities and shattering three hundred cedars.
slides.hebrewSource: בִּמְקוֹמֵנוּ מַפְשִׁיטִין אֶת הַמֵּתָה וּמַלְבִּישִׁין אֶת הַחַי

slides.title: 📅 Three Times a Year to Gather and Tithe
slides.subtitle: The new mishna's calendar, per Rabbi Akiva

steps.content: 1️⃣ Adjacent to Passover — animals born since the last gathering are counted and tithed
2️⃣ Adjacent to Shavuot — a second gathering time
3️⃣ Adjacent to Sukkot — a third and final gathering time for the year
4️⃣ Alternative views follow (ben Azzai; R' Elazar and R' Shimon) with different exact dates, to be explored next

callout.label: Why three?
callout.text: This sets up the next daf's explanation: so that untithed, permissible-to-eat animals remain available for those making pilgrimage to Jerusalem for each festival.

summary.principle: Animal tithe follows the same categorical exclusions as sacrificial offerings (crossbred, tereifa, caesarean, underage, orphan) via a shared verbal analogy, yet — because a mere blemish never disqualifies tithe — animals disqualified from the altar for licentiousness or idolatry are still tithed.

flowSteps.content: 🐕 Both of Rabbi Yoḥanan's teachings (Jubilee and purchased fetuses) were independently necessary
🚫 Mishna excludes kilayim, tereifa, caesarean birth, underage, and orphaned animals from tithe

columns.content: 🐄 Yet animals disqualified for licentiousness/idolatry ARE still tithed, since blemishes don't disqualify tithe
📅 Three yearly gathering times (Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot) begin the new mishna

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: tithe's exclusions track birth-status and species, not moral or ritual disqualifications that stem from a mere blemish standard

quiz.q: Why does the mishna exclude an 'orphan' animal — one whose mother died while giving birth to it — from animal tithe?
o: Because orphans are always weaker animals
The exclusion is derived from 'under its mother' (Leviticus 22:27), applied to tithe via a verbal analogy of 'under'
Because such animals cannot survive to be tithed
There is no such exclusion in the mishna
quiz.e: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka, derives all the tithe exclusions — including the orphan — through a verbal analogy between 'under the rod' (tithe) and 'under its mother' (sacrificial offerings).

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehoshua's definition in the mishna, when is a newborn animal NOT considered an 'orphan' despite its mother having been slaughtered during birth?
o: Never — any animal whose mother died is always an orphan
When the mother's hide still exists (survives) at the time of birth
Only if the father is still alive
Only during the summer months
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehoshua rules that even if the mother was slaughtered, the newborn is not considered an orphan as long as the mother's hide is present — as later testimony reveals, the hide could be used to clothe and effectively 'replace' the mother for the newborn.

quiz.q: Why are animals disqualified from being sacrificed due to licentiousness (e.g., bestiality) or idol worship nevertheless included in animal tithe?
o: Because tithe has no disqualifications at all
Because animal tithe is never disqualified by a mere physical blemish, and 'corruption'-based disqualifications only apply wherever a blemish would also disqualify
Because the Torah explicitly commands their inclusion by name
Because these animals are considered more valuable
quiz.e: The Gemara reasons that the disqualifications for licentiousness or idolatry are linked textually to blemish-disqualification; since animal tithe is exempt from blemish-disqualification ('he shall not inspect between good and bad'), it is likewise exempt from these corruption-based disqualifications.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda (in the name of Rabbi Shimon), why are a tumtum and an androginus excluded from animal tithe, unlike other disqualified animals?
o: They are considered too valuable to tithe
Their sex is uncertain, and sacrificial animals by definition require a definite male or female — similar to how a tereifa is excluded
They are excluded only outside Eretz Yisrael
There is no such exclusion — they are always included
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda holds that a tumtum (indeterminate sex) or androginus (both sexes) represents a genuine uncertainty about the animal's category, which sacrificial law excludes just as it excludes a tereifa — via the same 'under' verbal analogy.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Akiva in the new mishna, how many times per year are animals gathered and tithed, and around which festivals?
o: Once a year, before Passover only
Three times: adjacent to Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot
Twelve times, once each month
Two times: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva's mishna establishes three yearly gathering times for animal tithe, timed adjacent to each of the three pilgrimage festivals: Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot.
